No Single Neuron of Failure: Distributed Safety Alignment Against White-Box Attacks

Distributed safety alignment trains compensatory capacity instead of concentrating refusal behavior in a fragile internal bottleneck.

Xie Simiao

August 2, 2026 ·Preprint ·3-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

Distributed Safety Alignment examines a vulnerability of open-weight models: an attacker who can manipulate internal neurons may disable a narrow refusal mechanism. DSA first uses activation and loss-gradient information to locate refusal-related FFN coordinates, then perturbs those coordinates during realignment.

Targeted masking and stochastic dropout encourage the model to recruit compensatory capacity. The objective is to make refusal less dependent on a small, easily disrupted set of components, while retaining the language and multimodal abilities that make the model useful.

TaylorDirection-aware localization
Mask + dropComplementary perturbations
RedundancyTarget of safety realignment

A safety mechanism becomes more resilient when its useful computation has trained alternatives.

Why this matters

High refusal accuracy on an intact model does not reveal how concentrated the underlying mechanism is. If a small intervention can remove most of that behavior, ordinary output evaluations can overstate the robustness of the alignment.

How it works

  1. Localize refusal-related FFN coordinates with a direction-aware first-order Taylor score combining activations and loss gradients.
  2. Apply targeted deterministic masking and stochastic dropout during safety realignment.
  3. Evaluate disruption of dominant and compensatory neurons alongside general language and multimodal utility.

What the study finds

The paper compares robustness under neuron-pruning attacks, studies the contribution of masking and dropout, and tracks newly recruited refusal routes under successive disruptions. Its quantitative ablations pair attack success rates with ARC utility, making robustness and capability preservation visible together.

What this means

The study connects interpretability to fault tolerance. Finding a compact mechanism can help explain a behavior, while also revealing where that behavior is fragile. Training alternative computational support turns that diagnosis into a concrete alignment objective.

Redundancy is useful when the alternatives preserve the intended decision rather than merely move the same dependency. Successive-intervention analyses help test that distinction. The reported robustness is defined by the tested attacks and budgets, motivating broader adaptive evaluations of the trained alternatives.
